newsitem.title: USA: U.S. is sending an envoy to Taleban in Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. is sending an envoy to Taleban in Afghanistan.

text.p: The U.S. government put out feelers on Tuesday to the Taleban militia, which has seized most of Afghanistan, announcing it would send a diplomat shortly to talk to the new rulers in Kabul.
Among the tasks of the envoy will be to assess prospects for re-staffing the U.S. Embassy in the Afghan capital, which was evacuated seven years ago, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
Burns told reporters the diplomat would travel to Kabul "in the next couple of days." Citing security reasons, he declined to name the official or say where he would be travelling from.

"The purpose of his mission will be to make contact with the Taleban leadership, to essentially investigate the situation in Kabul, see if a government is being formed" and convey U.S. concerns about Taleban actions so far, Burns said.
Another aim was "to see if at some point in the future it's wise to at least have embassy officials go back in and re-establish an American embassy presence in Kabul," he said.

The United States never broke off relations with Afghanistan but pulled out all embassy staff after Soviet forces withdrew from the country in 1989, leading to a civil war between rebel factions that has continued ever since.

In Kabul, the Taleban's acting deputy foreign minister, Sher Mohammed Stanakzai, said the movement wanted good relations with neighbouring countries and with the United States and invited them to reopen their embassies in Kabul.

Despite the Islamic fundamentalist nature of the Taleban, Washington has clearly been tempted by the idea of a government that might be able to establish control over the whole country, devastated by years of fighting.

Reports from Kabul say the Taleban currently controls about three-quarters of Afghanistan. Stanakzai said on Tuesday the movement had set up a six-man council to run the country until the military situation became clear.

Although Afghanistan's strategic importance to the United States has declined since the end of the Cold War, Washington has abiding concerns about the country as a breeding ground for Islamic guerrillas and source of hard drugs.

Burns said the United States had been in touch with the Taleban twice before this year through Robin Raphel, assistant secretary of state for South Asian affairs, including once in a provincial Afghan city. He said Raphel would not be the official now going to Kabul.

Burns reiterated U.S. concerns over the Taleban's human rights practices, including its summary execution of former president Najibullah after it captured Kabul last week, and its imposition of tough restrictions on women.
"Those issues will be mentioned in our first official contacts with the Taleban," he said. But he said it remained to be seen whether Taleban would extend its authority over the whole of Afghanistan.

Burns said the Taleban, a one-time band of Islamic student vigilantes, had been an army so far and not a government. "We will have to judge them by their actions, but we're not going to prejudge what their actions might be," he said.
Although the United States has had no diplomats stationed in Kabul in recent years, Afghanistan has continued to staff its embassy in Washington.

Officials there were not available for comment Tuesday, but a statement by ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani read at the United Nations on Monday said his government's diplomatic and consular missions would continue to represent Afghanistan.
U.S. officials said they understood the Taleban had said it would replace staff at the country's embassies.
